etymology: From the Middle English bigilen, an intensive of guile (Old French guile, “craft, deceit”); hence to deceive by craft rather than by force, to cheat with fair words, to lead a man astray while he thinks himself well led.
biblical_def: To beguile is to deceive by craft — not the blunt lie that announces itself, but the subtile winning of a soul by enticing words, so that the victim walks willingly into the snare. The word enters Scripture at the Fall and never loses that smell of the serpent. Arraigned before God, Eve answers, “The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat” (Gen 3:13). He did not overpower her; he questioned, then contradicted, then made the forbidden fruit look like wisdom. Paul reaches back to that first beguiling as the pattern of every heresy since: “I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ” (2Co 11:3). Note what is threatened — not the mind’s intelligence but its simplicity, the plain childlike hold upon Christ that craft is forever complicating. Men beguile too. The Gibeonites came with mouldy bread and clouted shoes, and Joshua asks, “Wherefore have ye beguiled us?” (Jos 9:22), for he had taken their word and “asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD.” Laban beguiled Jacob with Leah; the false teacher at Colosse would “beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels” (Col 2:18). So the word marks the devil’s chosen method against the church: not the sword, but the smooth tongue; not open war, but enticing words.
webster_summary: To deceive by craft or subtilty; to cheat with fair words; to lead astray while seeming to lead well.
webster_full: BEGUILE, to delude; to deceive; to impose on by artifice or craft.
An intensive of guile, “craft, deceit, cunning.”
It denotes deception by subtilty rather than by force or open falsehood.
The serpent beguiled Eve, and so corrupted her from simplicity (Gen 3:13; 2Co 11:3).
To beguile a man of his reward is to cheat him of it by fair pretence (Col 2:18).
scriptures: Gen 3:13
And the LORD God said unto the woman, What is this that thou hast done? And the woman said, The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat.
Jos 9:22
And Joshua called for them, and he spake unto them, saying, Wherefore have ye beguiled us, saying, We are very far from you; when ye dwell among us?
But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.
Col 2:18
Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind,
corruption_summary: A live corruption, and the oldest: the serpent’s method is not contradiction first but the question — yea, hath God said? — and the age has learned it well.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a corruption still at work, and Scripture names its author. The serpent did not begin by denying God’s word; he began by querying it — yea, hath God said? — loosening the text before he dared contradict it, then re-describing the LORD’s plain prohibition as a grudging restraint upon a woman’s becoming. That is beguiling, and it is the working method of every teacher who comes to Scripture to ask whether it really says what it says, who makes the clear text uncertain and the uncertain text authoritative, and who offers the fruit as enlightenment. Paul calls it what it is: enticing words (Col 2:4), by which men are beguiled while they congratulate themselves on their subtilty.

The mark of the beguiler is that he flatters where he should warn. At Colosse the error wore the dress of humility — a voluntary lowliness, a worshipping of angels, a claim to have seen what he had not seen — and Paul says it would beguile the saints of their very reward. So the false teacher rarely arrives denying Christ outright; he arrives adding to Him, offering a deeper thing than the simplicity that is in Christ, and the soul that follows finds too late it has been cheated. The guard is not cleverness but simplicity: to hold fast the plain word of God, to ask counsel at His mouth as Joshua failed to do with the Gibeonites, and to suspect every voice that begins by asking whether God really said.
roots_summary: The word means to deceive by craft or subtilty, to cheat with fair and enticing words.
roots_lines: Beguile — Middle English bigilen, an intensive of guile.
From Old French guile, “craft, deceit, cunning.”
It denotes deceiving by subtilty, not by force or open lie.
The serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty (Gen 3:13; 2Co 11:3).
To beguile of a reward is to cheat a man of it by fair pretence (Col 2:18).
usage: The serpent beguiled Eve: he questioned the word before he dared contradict it.
Beguiling aims not at the mind’s strength but at its simplicity toward Christ.
Let no man beguile you of your reward with a voluntary humility and enticing words.

etymology: From the Old French espier, “to watch, to spy out,” of Germanic root and akin to our spy; hence to catch sight of, to descry at a distance, to search a thing out with the eye.
biblical_def: To espy is to catch sight of — to search out with the eye, whether by a startled glance or by a deliberate reconnaissance. Both senses are in Scripture. In Egypt, one of Joseph’s brethren opened his sack in the inn “and he espied his money; for, behold, it was in his sack’s mouth” (Gen 42:27) — a sudden sight that made their hearts fail them, for grace returned to guilty men looks at first like a trap. Jeremiah bids the inhabitant of Aroer “stand by the way, and espy” (Jer 48:19), to watch the road and ask the fugitives what is done: the watchman’s work, seeing the judgment before it arrives. Chiefly the word belongs to Caleb: “Forty years old was I when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadeshbarnea to espy out the land; and I brought him word again as it was in mine heart” (Jos 14:7). Twelve men espied the same hills, the same walled cities, the same giants; ten brought back an evil report and one brought back God. The eye reports what the heart believes. But the word’s deepest use is not of man at all. Ezekiel says the LORD brought Israel “into a land that I had espied for them, flowing with milk and honey, which is the glory of all lands” (Eze 20:6). Before ever a spy crossed the border, God had surveyed the inheritance and chosen it for His people.
webster_summary: To catch sight of; to descry; to search out or discover with the eye.
webster_full: ESPY, to see at a distance; to descry; to discover by the eye.
From Old French espier, “to watch, to spy out”; akin to spy.
It denotes both a sudden catching of sight and a deliberate searching out.
Moses sent Caleb to espy out the land of Canaan (Jos 14:7).
The LORD Himself espied the land for His people beforehand (Eze 20:6).
scriptures: And as one of them opened his sack to give his ass provender in the inn, he espied his money; for, behold, it was in his sack's mouth.
Jos 14:7
Forty years old was I when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadeshbarnea to espy out the land; and I brought him word again as it was in mine heart.
O inhabitant of Aroer, stand by the way, and espy; ask him that fleeth, and her that escapeth, and say, What is done?
Eze 20:6
In the day that I lifted up mine hand unto them, to bring them forth of the land of Egypt into a land that I had espied for them, flowing with milk and honey, which is the glory of all lands:
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a plain word for catching sight; it recovers that the eye reports what the heart believes, and that God espied the inheritance first.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the conceit that seeing is believing. Twelve men were sent to espy out Canaan, and twelve men saw the same land — the same clusters of Eshcol, the same walled cities, the same sons of Anak. Ten espied and said, We be not able; Caleb espied and brought word again as it was in his heart, We are well able to overcome it. The difference was not in the eye but in the heart behind the eye. Unbelief looks at giants and forgets God; faith looks at giants and remembers Him. Every man reports the land he was sent to see, but he reports it in the accent of what he believes about the LORD who sent him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God espied first. Ezekiel says the LORD brought His people into a land that He had espied for them, flowing with milk and honey, the glory of all lands — surveyed, chosen, and appointed before ever a spy set foot in it. The searching out of the twelve did not discover the inheritance; it only confirmed what God had already seen and given. So it is with every mercy: we come at last to espy what sovereign love long ago prepared, and the brethren who trembled at the money in the sack’s mouth found it was not a snare but a gift.
roots_summary: The word means to catch sight of, to descry, to search out with the eye.
roots_lines: Espy — Old French espier, “to watch, to spy out.”
Of Germanic root, and akin to the English spy.
It denotes catching sight of a thing, or searching it out deliberately.
Caleb was sent to espy out the land and brought word again in faith (Jos 14:7).
The LORD espied the land for His people before they saw it (Eze 20:6).
usage: He espied his money in the sack’s mouth: returning mercy first looked like a snare.
Twelve espied one land; the eye reported what the heart believed about God.
The LORD espied the inheritance for His people before ever a spy crossed the border.

etymology: The older form of graft, from Old French grafe, from Latin graphium and Greek graphion, “a writing style or stylus” — so named because the cut scion is shaped like a pointed pen; hence to insert a shoot of one tree into the stock of another, that it may live by a root not its own.
biblical_def: To graff is the gardener’s art: to cut a living shoot and set it into the stock of another tree, that it may draw sap from a root it never grew. The KJV keeps the old spelling, and Paul makes the word carry the whole mystery of Jew and Gentile in Romans 11. The olive tree is Israel; some of the natural branches were broken off through unbelief; and the Gentile believer — a shoot of the wild olive, worthless stock, bearing nothing fit for the altar — “wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree” (Rom 11:17). Mark the direction. The wild branch does not improve the tree; the tree sustains the branch. Paul presses it: thou bearest not the root, but the root thee, and “because of unbelief they were broken off, and thou standest by faith. Be not highminded, but fear.” The grafting is “contrary to nature” (Rom 11:24), for husbandmen graff the good shoot into the wild stock, never the reverse — but grace works backwards, taking what is wild and worthless and binding it into the covenant root. And the tree is one, not two: “God is able to graff them in again” (Rom 11:23), for the same door of faith stands open to the natural branches. One olive, one root, one people of God, and every branch in it — wild or natural — standing there by faith alone.
webster_summary: To insert a shoot of one tree into the stock of another, that it may live by that root; in Romans 11, the ingrafting of the Gentiles into the olive tree.
webster_full: GRAFF, the older form of graft; to insert a scion or shoot into a stock.
From Latin graphium, “a stylus,” the cut shoot resembling a pointed pen.
The graffed branch lives not by its own root but by the stock that bears it.
The wild olive was graffed in and partakes of the root and fatness (Rom 11:17).
The grafting is contrary to nature, for grace takes the wild and makes it fruitful (Rom 11:24).
scriptures: And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree;
Thou wilt say then, The branches were broken off, that I might be graffed in.
And they also, if they abide not still in unbelief, shall be graffed in: for God is able to graff them in again.

For if thou wert cut out of the olive tree which is wild by nature, and wert graffed contrary to nature into a good olive tree: how much more shall these, which be the natural branches, be graffed into their own olive tree?
corruption_summary: A live corruption on two sides: the Gentile boast that the church simply displaced Israel, and the dispensational cutting of one olive tree into two.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul anticipated the corruption and forbade it in advance. The Gentile says, “The branches were broken off, that I might be graffed in” (Rom 11:19) — true enough as a fact, and deadly as a boast. So the apostle answers, Boast not against the branches; thou bearest not the root, but the root thee. Wherever the church has read her ingrafting as a warrant to despise the natural branches, wherever a supersessionist triumph has hardened into contempt for the Jew, she has spoken the very sentence Romans 11 puts in the mouth of the highminded and rebukes. The wild olive contributed nothing to the tree but its wildness. Grace graffed it in; grace can break it off; and the branch that boasts against the root has forgotten which end of the graft is alive.

The opposite error cuts one tree into two. Dispensational premillennialism — a nineteenth-century novelty of Darby and Scofield, unknown to any Reformation confession — keeps Israel and the church as two peoples with two destinies, which is precisely the arithmetic Paul’s figure forbids. There is one olive tree, one root, one fatness. The natural branches were broken off by unbelief, not by nationality, and “God is able to graff them in again” by the same faith that graffed the Gentile. This is the discipline of the metaphor: no branch stands by descent, and no branch stands by merit. Israel fell by unbelief; the Gentile stands by faith; both stand or fall in one tree, and the husbandman is God.
roots_summary: The word means to insert a shoot into another stock, that it may live by a root not its own.
roots_lines: Graff — the older English form of graft.
From Old French grafe, Latin graphium, Greek graphion, “a stylus.”
So called because the cut scion is shaped like a pointed pen.
The wild olive branch is graffed in and partakes of the root (Rom 11:17).
The grafting is contrary to nature, being the work of grace (Rom 11:24).
usage: Thou bearest not the root, but the root thee — the graffed branch owes all to the stock.
Contrary to nature: grace graffs the wild and worthless shoot into the good olive tree.
God is able to graff them in again — one tree, one root, and every branch there by faith.

etymology: From the Old English hladan, “to load, to heap up, to draw”; hence to load, to burden, to lay a weight upon a beast or a back. Its past is laded and its participle laden.
biblical_def: To lade is to load — to lay a burden on a beast or a back. Most often it is honest labour: “Lade your beasts, and go, get you unto the land of Canaan” (Gen 45:17), says Pharaoh, and the asses go out heaped with the good things of Egypt to a famished father. Nehemiah saw men “lading asses” on the sabbath and testified against them, for the day of God is not a day for loading. But Scripture soon turns the word inward, from the beast’s back to the soul’s. Isaiah cries, “Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity” (Isa 1:4) — guilt is a freight, and a nation staggers under it. And our Lord lays the word like a whip across the shoulders of the religious: “Woe unto you also, ye lawyers! for ye lade men with burdens grievous to be borne, and ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers” (Luk 11:46). That is the whole indictment of legalism in one sentence — men who pile the load and will not lift a finger under it, who bind on consciences what God never bound, and who are heavy with rules and light with mercy. Over against every such lader stands the Saviour, whose call is not to load but to unload: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Mat 11:28). The scribes lade; Christ unlades. His yoke is easy and His burden is light, because He carried the weight Himself.
webster_summary: To load; to burden; to lay a weight upon a beast or a back; participle laden.
webster_full: LADE, to load; to put on a burden; to charge with a freight.
From the Saxon hladan, “to load, to heap, to draw.”
Past laded; participle laden, as a people laden with iniquity (Isa 1:4).
The lawyers laded men with burdens grievous to be borne (Luk 11:46).
Christ calls the heavy laden to Himself for rest (Mat 11:28).
scriptures: And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, Say unto thy brethren, This do ye; lade your beasts, and go, get you unto the land of Canaan;
Isa 1:4

Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, a seed of evildoers, children that are corrupters: they have forsaken the LORD, they have provoked the Holy One of Israel unto anger, they are gone away backward.
And he said, Woe unto you also, ye lawyers! for ye lade men with burdens grievous to be borne, and ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
corruption_summary: A live corruption, and an old one: the lawyers lade men with burdens God never laid, and touch them not with one of their fingers.
corruption_paragraphs: The woe our Lord pronounced on the lawyers is the standing rebuke of legalism in every age. They laded men with burdens grievous to be borne — hedges about the law, traditions with the force of commandments, scruples multiplied until religion became a freight no back could carry — and touched not the burdens with one of their fingers. That is the mark of the false teacher: he is rigorous with other men’s consciences and lenient with his own. Wherever a church binds where God has not bound, whether by ceremony, by rule, or by the private standards of the strong pressed upon the weak, it has taken up the lawyer’s trade and laded the flock it was called to feed.

The corruption has a mirror image, and it is no better: the teacher who lifts every burden God did lay, and calls the unlading grace. Isaiah’s nation was laden with iniquity and did not know it, and the man who tells a laden sinner he carries nothing has not eased him but blinded him. The gospel does not deny the weight; it removes it, and only Christ can. He alone says, Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest — for the burden the lawyers piled on other men, and the guilt Isaiah’s people staggered under, He took upon Himself and bore up the hill to Calvary. His yoke is easy because He carried the load.
roots_summary: The word means to load, to burden, to lay a weight upon a beast or a back.
roots_lines: Lade — Old English hladan, “to load, to heap, to draw.”
It denotes laying a freight or burden upon a beast or a man.
Its participle is laden, as a people laden with iniquity (Isa 1:4).
The lawyers lade men with burdens they will not touch (Luk 11:46).
Christ unlades the heavy laden and gives them rest (Mat 11:28).
usage: Lade your beasts and go: the asses went out heaped with the good things of Egypt.
Ye lade men with burdens grievous to be borne, and touch them not with one finger.
The scribes lade and Christ unlades: come unto me, all ye that are heavy laden.

etymology: From the Latin vexare, “to shake, to jolt, to harass,” through the Old French vexer; hence to trouble, to harass, to afflict, to grieve — properly a shaking of a thing that will not let it rest.
biblical_def: To vex is to shake a thing until it cannot rest — to harass, to trouble, to grieve. The KJV uses it far more broadly than our thin modern “annoy,” and it runs through four great courses. First, it is forbidden between men, and the law guards the defenceless with it: “Thou shalt neither vex a stranger, nor oppress him: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt” (Exo 22:21) — and Ezekiel indicts a city that vexed the fatherless and the widow. Second, it names the emptiness of the world: Solomon looked on all the works done under the sun, “and, behold, all is vanity and vexation of spirit” (Ecc 1:14). Life apart from God does not merely disappoint; it agitates, a chasing of wind that leaves the soul shaken. Third, and most solemnly, sin vexes God Himself: “But they rebelled, and vexed his holy Spirit: therefore he was turned to be their enemy” (Isa 63:10). The Spirit who bore Israel through the wilderness was grieved by the people He carried. Fourth, the word names the tyranny of devils: a woman of Canaan cried, “my daughter is grievously vexed with a devil” (Mat 15:22), and Christ healed all that were vexed with unclean spirits. Peter adds the noblest use, of Lot, whose righteous soul was vexed from day to day in Sodom — a holy vexation, the shaking of a saint who cannot sit easy where God is dishonoured.
webster_summary: To trouble, harass, or afflict; to shake or agitate a thing so that it cannot rest.
webster_full: VEX, to irritate; to harass; to trouble; to afflict; to disquiet.
From the Latin vexare, “to shake, to jolt, to harass.”
The law forbids vexing the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow (Exo 22:21).
All under the sun is vanity and vexation of spirit (Ecc 1:14).
Israel rebelled and vexed His holy Spirit (Isa 63:10).
scriptures: Thou shalt neither vex a stranger, nor oppress him: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.
Ecc 1:14
I have seen all the works that are done under the sun; and, behold, all is vanity and vexation of spirit.
But they rebelled, and vexed his holy Spirit: therefore he was turned to be their enemy, and he fought against them.
And, behold, a woman of Canaan came out of the same coasts, and cried unto him, saying, Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou Son of David; my daughter is grievously vexed with a devil.
corruption_summary: A live misuse: the age has shrunk vexation to mere annoyance, and counsels the righteous soul never to be vexed at the sin it lives among.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions ride on this word. The first is a shrinking of it. We have made vex a small thing — a nuisance, an irritation — and so we read past the weight of Isaiah’s charge that Israel rebelled and vexed His holy Spirit. That is not a peevish God taking offence; the impassible God of Scripture is not moved as a man is moved, but He speaks so that we may feel what sin is: a grieving of the very Spirit who bore His people through the wilderness. To keep the word small is to keep sin small, and a small sin needs no cross.

The second is the counsel, urged on every side, that the believer ought not to be vexed at all — that a righteous soul troubled by the sin around it is merely censorious, and that peace with Sodom is a virtue. Peter says otherwise: Lot’s righteous soul was vexed from day to day with the unlawful deeds he saw and heard, and Peter records it not as his fault but as the proof he was righteous and the ground of his deliverance. A conscience that has ceased to be shaken by what shakes God has not grown charitable; it has grown numb. The saint is forbidden to vex the stranger and forbidden to be at ease in Sodom, and the same law commands both.
roots_summary: The word means to shake, harass, or trouble a thing so that it cannot rest.
roots_lines: Vex — from Latin vexare, “to shake, to jolt, to harass.”
It denotes troubling or agitating, far more than our modern “annoy.”
The law forbids vexing the stranger and the fatherless (Exo 22:21).
The world’s labour is vanity and vexation of spirit (Ecc 1:14).
Rebellion vexes the holy Spirit of God Himself (Isa 63:10).
usage: Thou shalt neither vex a stranger nor oppress him: the law guards the defenceless.
All is vanity and vexation of spirit — the world does not merely disappoint, it shakes.
Lot’s righteous soul was vexed in Sodom: a saint cannot sit easy where God is dishonoured.

etymology: From the Old English sūpan, “to sip, to swallow,” reinforced by the Old French souper; hence to take the evening meal, to eat supper — the settled, unhurried table at the end of the day’s work.
biblical_def: To sup is to take supper — not a snatched bite but the evening meal, the long table when the work is done, the meal of intimacy and rest. The word keeps its household plainness: the master says to the servant come in from the field, “Make ready wherewith I may sup, and gird thyself, and serve me” (Luk 17:8), and our Lord uses it to teach that the servant claims no thanks for doing what was commanded. It marks the holiest table in Scripture’s history: “After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood” (1Co 11:25). The cup came after supper — the paschal meal finished, the old covenant fulfilled at its own table, and a new testament in His blood set in its place. From that night the church has supped at the Lord’s table, where Christ is truly present to faith and feeds His people, though the bread be bread still. Then the word rises to the promise: “Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me” (Rev 3:20). To a lukewarm church that had shut her Lord outside, Christ offers not a rebuke only but a supper. And the whole of it runs toward one board at the end of history: “Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Rev 19:9).
webster_summary: To take the evening meal; to eat supper; the settled table of rest and fellowship at day’s end.
webster_full: SUP, to take supper; to eat the evening repast.
From the Saxon sūpan, “to sip, to swallow,” and Old French souper.
It denotes the settled meal at the end of labour, not a hasty bite.
Christ took the cup when He had supped, instituting the new testament (1Co 11:25).
He offers to come in and sup with him that opens the door (Rev 3:20).
scriptures: Luk 17:8
And will not rather say unto him, Make ready wherewith I may sup, and gird thyself, and serve me, till I have eaten and drunken; and afterward thou shalt eat and drink?
After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me.
Rev 3:20
Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.
Rev 19:9
And he saith unto me, Write, Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb. And he saith unto me, These are the true sayings of God.
corruption_summary: A live corruption of one verse: Rev 3:20 is a summons to a lukewarm church, not a sentimental proof-text for the sinner’s decision to let Christ in.
corruption_paragraphs: No verse with this word has been wrenched further from its place than Revelation 3:20. It is preached as though Christ stood powerless outside the unbeliever’s heart, waiting on a decision He cannot make and hoping for a latch He cannot lift — the whole of salvation hanging on the creature’s turn of the handle. But read the address: this letter is written to the church at Laodicea, lukewarm, rich and increased with goods, that had put her own Lord out of doors. The knocking is Christ recalling a backslidden congregation to His table, not a Saviour begging admission to a heart He is unable to enter. Scripture nowhere leaves the door in the sinner’s hand: the LORD opened Lydia’s heart, that she attended unto the things spoken of Paul, and the same effectual grace opens every door that opens at all.

Restore the verse and it grows greater, not smaller. The Christ who knocks is the sovereign Lord who counsels Laodicea to buy of Him gold tried in the fire and white raiment; He rebukes and chastens whom He loves; and the door that opens, opens because He gave the hearing ear to the voice outside it. Then the promise is not a bargain but a banquet: I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me — the long evening table, the meal of rest and intimacy with the risen Christ, pledged now at the Lord’s Supper and consummated at the marriage supper of the Lamb. He does not knock to be let in on our terms; He knocks because He has determined to sup.
roots_summary: The word means to take the evening meal, the settled table of rest and fellowship.
roots_lines: Sup — Old English sūpan, “to sip, to swallow.”
Reinforced by Old French souper, “to take the evening meal.”
It denotes the unhurried table when the day’s labour is done.
The cup of the new testament was taken when He had supped (1Co 11:25).
Christ promises to come in and sup with him that opens (Rev 3:20).
usage: He took the cup when He had supped: the paschal table finished, the new testament begun.
Rev 3:20 knocks at a lukewarm church’s door, not at a heart that can open itself.
Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb.

etymology: The old past tense of tread, from the Old English tredan, “to step, to walk upon”; the KJV’s trode is our trod, and it carries most often the sense of trampling — setting the foot upon a thing in scorn, in haste, or in judgment.
biblical_def: Trode is the Authorized Version’s past tense of tread, and it is seldom a gentle word. Sometimes it is honest work: at Shechem they “gathered their vineyards, and trode the grapes, and made merry, and went into the house of their god” (Jdg 9:27) — and even there the treading ends in drunken feasting and the cursing of Abimelech, labour turned to riot. More often it is judgment underfoot. Jehu commanded that Jezebel be thrown down, “and he trode her under foot” (2Ki 9:33), and the dogs ate her as the word of the LORD by Elijah had said. It carries the sting of Jehoash’s parable to proud Amaziah: the thistle of Lebanon presumed to ask the cedar’s daughter for his son, “and there passed by a wild beast that was in Lebanon, and trode down the thistle” (2Ki 14:9). Pride reaches for the cedar and is flattened by a passing beast. And it names the crush of the crowd about our Lord: an innumerable multitude was gathered, “insomuch that they trode one upon another” (Luk 12:1) — and to that trampling throng He began, Beware ye of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. Men who tread each other down to hear a sermon need that sermon most. The word reaches its height in Isaiah, where the Messiah says, “I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me.”
webster_summary: The old past tense of tread: trod; to have set the foot upon, most often to have trampled down.
webster_full: TRODE, the preterit of tread; our trod.
From the Saxon tredan, “to step, to walk or set the foot upon.”
It commonly bears the sense of trampling, in scorn or in judgment.
They trode the grapes in the vineyards of Shechem (Jdg 9:27).
The multitude trode one upon another to come at Christ (Luk 12:1).
scriptures: Jdg 9:27
And they went out into the fields, and gathered their vineyards, and trode the grapes, and made merry, and went into the house of their god, and did eat and drink, and cursed Abimelech.
And he said, Throw her down. So they threw her down: and some of her blood was sprinkled on the wall, and on the horses: and he trode her under foot.

And Jehoash the king of Israel sent to Amaziah king of Judah, saying, The thistle that was in Lebanon sent to the cedar that was in Lebanon, saying, Give thy daughter to my son to wife: and there passed by a wild beast that was in Lebanon, and trode down the thistle.
Luk 12:1

In the mean time, when there were gathered together an innumerable multitude of people, insomuch that they trode one upon another, he began to say unto his disciples first of all, Beware ye of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the old past of tread; it recovers the trampling of pride and the winepress Christ trode alone.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the trampling that religious eagerness can become. An innumerable multitude gathered to Christ and trode one upon another — men crushing their neighbours underfoot in their haste to hear — and His first word to them was, Beware ye of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. There is a way of pressing hard after the things of God that treads down the very neighbour the second commandment binds us to love, and the crowd that does it is the crowd most in need of the warning. So too the thistle of Jehoash’s parable, presuming upon the cedar and trodden down by a passing beast: pride reaches above its stature and is flattened without ceremony.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the winepress. Isaiah hears the Messiah say, “I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me” — and there is the gospel in a figure. The treading that saves us was done by One, unassisted, unaccompanied, His garments stained with the vintage of His own suffering. Jehu trode Jezebel under foot and the crowd trode one another, but Christ trode the press of the wrath of God alone, that His people might never be trodden down. Heb 10:29 sets the only alternative before us: to have trodden under foot the Son of God, and counted the blood of the covenant an unholy thing.
roots_summary: The word is the old past tense of tread, to set or trample the foot upon.
roots_lines: Trode — the KJV preterit of tread; our trod.
From Old English tredan, “to step, to walk upon.”
It most often denotes trampling, in scorn or in judgment.
Jehu trode Jezebel under foot, as Elijah had foretold (2Ki 9:33).
The Messiah trode the winepress alone, none with Him (Isa 63:3).
usage: They trode the grapes and made merry — and the vintage ended in riot and cursing.
A wild beast trode down the thistle: pride reaches for the cedar and is flattened.
They trode one upon another to hear Him, and He preached against hypocrisy.

etymology: From the Old French raser, “to scrape, to shave close,” from the Latin radere, “to scrape”; hence to level with the ground, to demolish so utterly that the very foundation is scraped bare. A KJV hapax, occurring but once.
biblical_def: To rase is to scrape a thing flat — not to damage a city but to unmake it, to shave it down until the foundation itself lies naked. It occurs but once in all Scripture, and once is enough. Among the rivers of Babylon the captives remember who cheered when Jerusalem fell: “Remember, O LORD, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem; who said, Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof” (Psa 137:7). The doubling is the horror of it — rase it, rase it — a chant, an urging on, the voice of men standing at a safe distance and calling for more. And these were Edom, the sons of Esau, Jacob’s own brother; the kinsman cheered the executioner. Note what the psalmist does with his fury. He does not sharpen a sword; he says, Remember, O LORD. The imprecation is a handing over: vengeance belongs to God, and the captive who cries for justice into God’s ear has already refused to take it into his own hand. The prophets answer the prayer — Samaria is made an heap of the field and her foundations discovered (Mic 1:6), and Edom is laid waste. Yet the awful symmetry is that Jerusalem herself would hear the sentence again from her own Lord, who wept as He said it: they shall “lay thee even with the ground… because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation” (Luk 19:44).
webster_summary: To level with the ground; to demolish utterly, scraping a city down to its foundation. A KJV hapax.
webster_full: RASE, to level with the ground; to overthrow; to destroy utterly.
From Latin radere, “to scrape,” through Old French raser.
It denotes not damaging but unmaking — scraping bare the very foundation.
It occurs but once in Scripture, a KJV hapax (Psa 137:7).
Edom cried, Rase it, rase it, in the day of Jerusalem’s fall.
scriptures: Remember, O LORD, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem; who said, Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof.
Mic 1:6
Therefore I will make Samaria as an heap of the field, and as plantings of a vineyard: and I will pour down the stones thereof into the valley, and I will discover the foundations thereof.
And shall lay thee even with the ground, and thy children within thee; and they shall not leave in thee one stone upon another; because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation.
Mat 24:2
And Jesus said unto them, See ye not all these things? verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a word for utter demolition; it recovers the sin of the cheering kinsman and the imprecation that hands vengeance to God.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the spectator’s sin. Edom did not burn Jerusalem; Babylon did. Edom stood by and cheered — Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof — and the LORD wrote their cry down against them as though the torch had been in their hand. They were kinsmen, the sons of Esau, brethren of Jacob; and there is no crueller voice than the relative at a safe distance urging on the ruin of his own blood. The age knows this sin well, though it has forgotten the word: the crowd that lends no hand but lends its voice, that would never strike the blow yet calls for it and calls for it twice. God does not distinguish as we do between the arm that destroys and the mouth that eggs it on.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what the psalmist did with his rage. He had every ground for vengeance and he took none; he said, Remember, O LORD. The imprecatory psalm is not the believer arming himself but the believer disarming himself — laying the whole burning case in the hands of the Judge of all the earth, who alone does right, and leaving it there. Vengeance is mine, saith the LORD; I will repay. And the last word is a warning against gloating, for the city Edom would have rased was rased indeed, and heard the sentence a second time from Christ Himself, who did not chant it but wept over it: not one stone left upon another, because she knew not the time of her visitation.
roots_summary: The word means to level with the ground, to demolish a city down to its foundation.
roots_lines: Rase — Old French raser, from Latin radere, “to scrape.”
It denotes scraping a city flat, bare to its very foundation.
A KJV hapax, occurring but once (Psa 137:7).
Edom chanted it against Jerusalem: Rase it, rase it.
The psalmist answers not with a sword but with “Remember, O LORD.”
usage: Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof — the cheer of a brother turned enemy.
Edom held no torch but lent its voice; God reckoned the cry as the deed.
Remember, O LORD: the imprecation hands vengeance to the Judge and keeps none back.

etymology: The KJV spelling of assuage, from the Old French asouagier, from a Latin root joining ad- (“to”) and suavis (“sweet, mild”); hence to soften, to mitigate, to abate — to make a raging thing sink down and grow still.
biblical_def: To asswage is to make a raging thing subside — to soften, to mitigate, to bring a flood or a grief down from its height. The KJV keeps the old spelling, and its first use is the greatest. When the world lay drowned and the ark rode a shoreless sea, we read: “And God remembered Noah, and every living thing, and all the cattle that was with him in the ark: and God made a wind to pass over the earth, and the waters asswaged” (Gen 8:1). Mark the order. The waters do not asswage because they have spent themselves; they asswage because God remembered. It is not that the LORD had forgotten — His remembering is His acting, the turning of covenant love toward His own — and at that instant a wind passes over the deep, as the Spirit once moved upon the face of the waters, and the flood sinks. The word’s other home is Job’s ash-heap, where it names a failure. Job tells his friends that were their places changed, “I would strengthen you with my mouth, and the moving of my lips should asswage your grief” (Job 16:5) — and then, of himself, “Though I speak, my grief is not asswaged: and though I forbear, what am I eased?” (Job 16:6). Miserable comforters are ye all. Words are the right instrument and yet they will not reach; speech does not asswage and silence does not either. Only the God who made the wind pass over the flood can bid a grief go down.
webster_summary: To soften, mitigate, or abate; to make a raging thing — a flood or a grief — sink down and grow still.
webster_full: ASSWAGE, the old spelling of assuage; to soften; to allay; to mitigate.
From Old French asouagier, akin to the Latin suavis, “sweet, mild.”
It denotes the sinking down of what has raged — waters, pain, or grief.
God made a wind to pass over the earth, and the waters asswaged (Gen 8:1).
Job’s grief was not asswaged, whether he spake or forbore (Job 16:6).
scriptures: Gen 8:1
And God remembered Noah, and every living thing, and all the cattle that was with him in the ark: and God made a wind to pass over the earth, and the waters asswaged;
Job 16:5
But I would strengthen you with my mouth, and the moving of my lips should asswage your grief.
Job 16:6
Though I speak, my grief is not asswaged: and though I forbear, what am I eased?
Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a word for the sinking of a flood; it recovers that grief is asswaged by the God who remembers, not by the words of miserable comforters.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes every confidence that grief can be talked down. Job’s three friends came with a technique and a theory, and he named them miserable comforters all; and when Job himself takes up the instrument he finds it broken in his hand — though I speak, my grief is not asswaged, and though I forbear, what am I eased? There is the whole failure of counsel that has no God in it. Speech will not asswage and silence will not asswage, and the sufferer is left where the friends found him. It is no kindness to promise a mourner that the right words, well arranged, will bid his sorrow sink; and it is a cruelty to reason him into guilt he does not bear, as Eliphaz did.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is who asswages. God remembered Noah — and the waters asswaged. The flood did not exhaust itself; it obeyed. A wind passed over the earth at the bidding of the God whose Spirit had moved upon the face of the waters at the first, and the deep that had covered the mountains began to sink. So the Christian brings his grief not to a method but to a Person: the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort, who comforteth us in all our tribulation — and He comforts us not for ourselves alone, but that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God.
roots_summary: The word means to soften or abate, to make a raging thing sink down and grow still.
roots_lines: Asswage — the KJV spelling of assuage.
From Old French asouagier, akin to Latin suavis, “sweet, mild.”
It denotes softening, mitigating, the sinking down of what has raged.
God remembered Noah, and the waters asswaged (Gen 8:1).
Neither speech nor silence asswaged Job’s grief (Job 16:6).
usage: God remembered Noah, and the waters asswaged: the flood sank because God acted.
Though I speak, my grief is not asswaged — words without God cannot bid sorrow down.
The God of all comfort asswages our tribulation, that we may comfort others with it.

etymology: From the Old French avochier, “to call upon, to summon as witness,” from the Latin advocare, “to call to” (ad- + vocare, “to call”); hence to declare openly, to avow, to affirm a thing solemnly and publicly as one’s own.
biblical_def: To avouch is to declare a thing openly and bind oneself to the declaration — to avow before witnesses, calling others to hear what one owns. The word occurs only twice in all Scripture, side by side, and it carries the covenant formula of the Old Testament: “Thou hast avouched the LORD this day to be thy God, and to walk in his ways, and to keep his statutes… And the LORD hath avouched thee this day to be his peculiar people” (Deu 26:17-18). Here is the covenant in one breath, and it is mutual — He is ours and we are His — but it is not equal, and the order is everything. Israel avouches the LORD only because the LORD first avouched Israel; she does not create the bond by her declaration but confesses one that sovereign love had already made. Nor is the avouching a private sentiment. It is a public, spoken, binding word committing the whole life — to walk in His ways and hearken unto His voice — with the promise that God will “make thee high above all nations… and that thou mayest be an holy people unto the LORD thy God” (Deu 26:19). Peter carries the very phrase into the church: “ye are… a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light” (1Pe 2:9). God avouches first; His people answer.
webster_summary: To declare openly; to avow; to affirm a thing solemnly and publicly as one’s own.
webster_full: AVOUCH, to affirm openly; to declare; to avow; to maintain a thing as one’s own.
From the Latin advocare, “to call to,” through Old French avochier.
It denotes not a private opinion but a public, binding declaration.
Israel avouched the LORD to be her God (Deu 26:17).
The LORD avouched Israel to be His peculiar people (Deu 26:18).
scriptures: Thou hast avouched the LORD this day to be thy God, and to walk in his ways, and to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments, and to hearken unto his voice:
And the LORD hath avouched thee this day to be his peculiar people, as he hath promised thee, and that thou shouldest keep all his commandments;
And to make thee high above all nations which he hath made, in praise, and in name, and in honour; and that thou mayest be an holy people unto the LORD thy God, as he hath spoken.
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the old covenant formula; it recovers that God avouched first, and that His covenant is no contract to be kept while convenient.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes a religion of private and unspoken sentiment. To avouch is to say a thing out loud, before witnesses, and to be held to it — and the age much prefers a faith that commits to nothing it must name. It prefers, too, the contract to the covenant: an arrangement entered for benefit, weighed while it serves, and dissolved when it ceases to please. But Deuteronomy 26 is not a bargain struck between parties of equal standing; it is the LORD binding a people to Himself and that people answering with their whole life — to walk in His ways, to keep His statutes, to hearken unto His voice. Where the covenant is downgraded to a contract, the marriage vow follows it down, and so does church membership, for both were modelled on this.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order of the two avouchings. Israel avouched the LORD to be her God; but the LORD avouched Israel to be His peculiar people, and He did it first. She did not make the covenant by confessing it; she confessed a covenant sovereign love had already made, for He did not set His love upon her because she was more in number than any people — she was the fewest of all — but because the LORD loved her. So the believer’s confession never creates his standing; it answers a God who chose him before the foundation of the world. We love him, because he first loved us; and we avouch Him, because He first avouched us.
roots_summary: The word means to declare openly and bind oneself to the declaration, to avow publicly.
roots_lines: Avouch — Old French avochier, from Latin advocare, “to call to.”
It denotes an open, public, binding declaration, not a private sentiment.
It occurs but twice in Scripture, in the covenant formula of Deu 26:17-18.
Israel avouched the LORD to be her God, and He avouched her His people.
God avouches first; the confession of His people is the answer.
usage: Thou hast avouched the LORD this day to be thy God — a public word, not a private mood.
The LORD hath avouched thee to be his peculiar people: He owns His own out loud.
God avouched first; our confession does not make the covenant but answers it.
